To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the levels of activity of all urea-cycle enzymes are increased in the livers of animals fed diets high in protein, and that this adaptation can largely be accounted for by differences in the actual contents of enzyme proteins.
the activity of each of the six urea cycle enzymes varies with the dietary protein intake of the rat.
the levels of all the enzymes of the urea cycle are increased in parallel with increasing dietary protein.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the adaptive characteristics of urea synthesis in the rat and with the mechanisms of adaptation to varying dietary intake of protein.
the mechanisms by which the rat adapts to changes in the level of protein in the diet.
the adaptive changes in urea cycle enzyme levels in the rat in response to differences between dietary protein.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the rat adapts to differing protein consumption largely by changing the level of enzyme protein in the liver, and that the changes are specific for the urea cycle enzymes.
the adaptive response to dietary protein is a result of the regulation of enzyme synthesis, and that the mechanism for this regulation is not a change in kinetic characteristics of the enzymes.

the adaptive response of the rat to differing protein intake involves changes in the level of enzyme protein in the liver for all enzymes of the urea cycle, and that these changes can be accounted for quantitatively on the basis of the levels of activity of each of the enzymes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, in adaptation to varying protein intake, the rate of ureal synthesis is controlled by the rate of synthesis of urea cycle enzyme protein, rather than by changes in the rate at which the enzymes are inactivated or by changes in the rates at which substrates are made available to the enzymes.
dietary protein regulates enzyme activity in the urea cycle by a mechanism involving the amount of enzyme protein present in the cell.

the mammal adapts to differing protein intake by varying the levels of urea cycle enzyme proteins, and that these changes are accomplished by altering rates of synthesis and degradation of enzyme proteins.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the adaptive characteristics of the urea cycle enzymes are very similar.
there is a direct correlation between dietary protein and the activity of the urea cycle enzymes.
the enzyme activities are regulated by a number of different mechanisms.
